newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Swedish commission leak heats up EMU debate.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Swedish commission leak heats up EMU debate.

text.p: The Swedish government's own commission of inquiry was said on Thursday to be set to reject membership of Europe's single currency, stoking controversy surrounding membership of the Exchange Rate Mechanism.

The daily Dagens Politik, quoting sources with access to the commission's findings, said it would recommend rejection of membership of the third phase of the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) when it announces its findings next Monday.

The team of academics led by Professor Lars Calmfors was set up by the Swedish government to examine the consequences for Sweden of EMU membership and its findings are expected to play an important role in Sweden's decision on EMU.

Dagens Politik said the commission had been unable to find any valid economic arguments for Swedish EMU membership and that it had concluded the proposed European currency, the Euro, risked being unstable and weak.

"Joint monetary and currency policies are necessary for those who want a more tightly knit union in Europe, but the case for EMU collapses without that desire for closer union," Dagens Poltik quoted the report as saying.
Calmfors commission member Ewa Rabinowicz told Reuters the newspaper report was "loose speculation."
Christina Nordberntsson, the secretary of the team, also said the report had no foundation in the work of the group.
If the commission does come out against Swedish membership of the single currency, its rejection will welcomed by Sweden's fervent Euro-scepticism.

The government has said a firm decision on whether to join the EMU will be taken in parliament late in 1997. This means that the matter will effectively be settled by the ruling Social Democrats' party congress in September next year.
Thus, the "thorough debate" called for by Prime Minister Goran Persson in August has begun to heat up.

Riksbank chairman and former SPD finance minister Kjell-Olof Feldt attracted sharp criticism from the centre and left of the political spectrum -- both bastions of EMU opposition -- when he on Monday repeated the central bank's generally pro-EMU stance.
Most vociferous among Feldt's critics was Centre Party leader Olof Johansson, whose party supports the minority Social Democrats in parliament on economic issues.
In an acrimonious media exchange, Johansson said Feldt should "step back into line," and not compromise what he regarded as the Riksbank's duty to remain neutral on the matter.
Feldt responded by asking whose line Johansson wanted him to step into, parliament's or the Centre Party's.
Whatever Persson and Finance Minister Erik Asbrink finally decide to do, and it is they who will ultimately settle the matter, their decision will be problematic.

At home, a decision to join will be deeply unpopular among th electorate. Recent polls have shown Swedes to be the European Union's most reluctant citizens, with only 32 percent approving the country's decision to join the Union.
Not only that, the fact that the decision will be made in the run-up to the September 1998 general election also plays into the hands of the anti single currency lobby.
On the other hand, Swedish recalcitrance on EMU would win it few friends in Brussels, where Sweden has already gained a reputation as a difficult customer.

EU financial mandarins have made it clear that they do not share Persson's view that two year's membership of the Exchange Rate Mechanism is not a strict prerequisite for eventual membership of the single currency.
Alexandre Lamfalussy, head of the precursor to the European Central Bank, pointedly remarked on a recent visit to Stockholm the Maastricht ERM criterion stands firm.
